metadata.title: Reading instruction and reading engagement and their relationship with Chinese students’ PISA reading performance: Evidence from B-S-J-Z, Hong Kong, and Chinese Taipei

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for three Chinese societies (B-S-J-Z, Hong Kong, and Chinese Taipei) and models students’ reading literacy scores as the dependent variable. The analytic sample is restricted to 15-year-old students in 9th and 10th grade who completed the computer-based reading assessment and the relevant student questionnaire indices, with school-level background variables included via a two-level HLM framework. The manuscript does not report the use of PISA complex survey weights (e.g., student/sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures, so it is unclear whether population-representative weighting was applied in estimation. Because the analysis is hierarchical linear modeling rather than ML, the paper’s weighting strategy is not described; readers should consult the PISA technical documentation for recommended weight variables when replicating the results.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is the PISA 2018 reading literacy score based on a combined literacy scale using the Rasch method, and the paper does not describe any explicit plausible-values (PV) workflow (e.g., PV1/PV averages or Rubin combining rules). Because the authors also do not report how missing questionnaire or index data were handled (e.g., complete-case vs imputation), the missing-data strategy is a reporting gap. Given PISA’s questionnaire nonresponse patterns, the absence of a documented missing-data approach limits transparency about potential bias.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 data restricted to three Chinese societies selected by OECD: Beijing-Shanghai-Jiangsu-Zhejiang (B-S-J-Z), Hong Kong, and Chinese Taipei. The sample consists of 15-year-old students in 9th and 10th grade from 720 schools total (362 in B-S-J-Z, 166 in Hong Kong, 192 in Chinese Taipei). The analysis includes students who have reading achievement (computer-based reading assessment) and the relevant student- and school-level questionnaire indices used to construct the instruction and reading engagement predictors; no additional exclusion rules (e.g., missingness thresholds) are reported.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (computer-based), 15-year-olds (B-S-J-Z, Hong Kong, Chinese Taipei)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-level HLM (Model 1 vs Model 2). Variance explained (between-school / within-school): B-S-J-Z Model 2 77.1% / 23.9%; Hong Kong 73.1% / 24.7%; Chinese Taipei 87.7% / 33.4%. Coefficients reported in Table 5 (significance via p-values).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading data for 15-year-olds in B-S-J-Z, Hong Kong, and Chinese Taipei, the study leveraged disciplinary climate, teacher support, teacher-directed instruction, metacognition of assessing credibility, and perceived reading difficulty to model reading achievement, finding that disciplinary climate and teacher support were significant positive predictors while teacher-directed instruction was a significant negative predictor across regions (with engagement effects strongest in Model 2). This indicates that strengthening classroom order and autonomy-supportive teacher practices, alongside explicit instruction and practice for credibility-checking strategies, may be more effective for reading performance than emphasizing teacher control alone, though the HLM results are correlational rather than causal.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2018 computer-based reading literacy for 15-year-olds from three Chinese societies (B-S-J-Z, Hong Kong, Chinese Taipei; total N=25,338 across 720 schools). Using a two-level hierarchical linear model (students nested in schools), the authors first estimate effects of background controls and seven instruction indices (TMQT-based: cognitive activation, classroom management/structure, supportive climate), then add six reading engagement indices (cognitive and non-cognitive engagement). In Model 1, disciplinary climate and teacher support are significant positive predictors, while teacher-directed instruction is a significant negative predictor across all three regions; teacher enthusiasm is not significant. In Model 2, metacognition of assessing credibility is the strongest positive engagement predictor across regions, while perceived reading difficulty is a significant negative predictor; joy of reading and metacognitive strategies (understanding/remembering and summarizing) are also positive. The paper reports variance explained and coefficients but does not document PV handling or missing-data treatment, and HLM provides associations rather than causal effects.
